AUS.culture: Australians love barbecues, beach days and footy, and their food scene blends British classics like meat pies with strong Asian and Mediterranean influences. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander traditions, from didgeridoo music to rock art, are the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.
AUS.history: Aboriginal Australians arrived by boat tens of thousands of years ago and built the world's oldest living cultures, with deep spiritual ties to the land called Country. British colonists arrived in 1788, first landing a convict fleet at Sydney Cove, and settlers spread across the continent, often with devastating effects on Indigenous communities. Separate colonies federated into the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901, and the country fought alongside the Allies in both world wars. Modern Australia is a wealthy multicultural nation, and in 2008 parliament formally apologized to the Stolen Generations of Indigenous children taken from their families.
AUS.funFact: Australia once lost a war to emus in 1932, when the army was sent to cull the birds and gave up after the emus kept outsmarting the soldiers.

famous: the Lord of the Rings film locations
NZL.culture: Maori culture shapes national life, from the haka war dance performed before rugby matches to the greeting 'kia ora', and hangi feasts are cooked in earth ovens. New Zealanders, who call themselves Kiwis, are famous for a love of rugby, tramping in the mountains and a dry, understated sense of humor.
NZL.history: Maori voyagers arrived from eastern Polynesia around the 1300s, navigating by stars and currents in great waka canoes. Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sighted the islands in 1642 and British settlement accelerated after the Treaty of Waitangi was signed with Maori chiefs in 1840, though later land conflicts left grievances that are still being settled today. New Zealand became a self-governing dominion in 1907 and a fully independent nation, pioneering women's suffrage in 1893 and its nuclear-free policy in the 1980s.
NZL.funFact: In 1893 New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women the right to vote.

famous: the coral Soft Coral Capital of the World
FJI.culture: Fijian life centers on the village and the kava ceremony, where yaqona root is pounded, mixed with water and shared from a communal bowl while everyone claps. Indian-Fijian cuisine added curries and roti to dishes like kokoda, raw fish marinated in coconut cream, and rugby is practically a religion.
FJI.history: Polynesian and Melanesian settlers reached Fiji more than 3,000 years ago, and for centuries the islands were known as the Cannibal Isles, feared by European sailors. Ratu Seru Cakobau united much of Fiji under one kingdom and ceded the islands to Britain in 1874, after which indentured laborers from India arrived to work sugarcane plantations, changing the country's makeup forever. Fiji became independent in 1970 and has since struggled through several military coups while remaining a Pacific powerhouse in sport and diplomacy.
FJI.funFact: Fiji's rugby sevens team performs a fearsome pre-match war cry called the cibi and won Olympic gold in Rio in 2016, the country's first ever medal.

PNG.culture: Papua New Guinea is one of the most culturally diverse places on Earth, with over 800 languages spoken by small communities who gather for huge singsing festivals of face paint, drums and dancing. People exchange shells, pigs and kina currency in traditional systems, and roughly 85 percent of the population still lives off the land.
PNG.history: Papuans have lived on the island for around 50,000 years, and highlanders independently invented agriculture some 7,000 years ago, among the earliest farming anywhere. European contact came slowly, with Germany and Britain splitting the eastern half of the island in the late 1800s, and Australia later administering the territory and fighting fierce battles against Japan there in World War II along the Kokoda Track. The unified country gained independence in 1975 and is still stitching together its thousands of communities into one modern state.
PNG.funFact: Scientists still regularly discover new species in PNG's forests, including a giant woolly rat and a frog that snored, and entire uncontacted communities may remain in the highlands.

famous: wrestling's Anoa'i family including The Rock
WSM.culture: Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, organizes life around extended families called aiga, village chiefs called matai and the church, with Sunday services and to'ona'i feasts of taro, palusami and roast pork. The siva dance and the legendary tattooing tradition, where the pe'a covers a man's body from waist to knee, carry huge cultural pride.
WSM.history: Samoans have voyaged and settled these islands for around 3,000 years, and their archipelago became a hub of Polynesian culture. Britain, Germany and the United States competed for influence until the Samoan crisis of the 1880s and 1890s, ending with the islands split in 1899 and Germany taking what is now independent Samoa. New Zealand occupied the islands in 1914 and administered them through the influenza epidemic of 1918 and the Mau independence movement, until Samoa became the first independent Polynesian nation of the modern era in 1962.
WSM.funFact: Samoa skipped December 30, 2011 entirely, jumping over the international date line so its work week would line up with Australia and New Zealand.

famous: NFL players from a tiny island
ASM.culture: Life follows fa'a Samoa like in independent Samoa, with matai chiefs, communal land and a strong church presence, but American touches like gridiron football and Spam are everywhere. Villages hold flag days and pageants, and traditional chiefs still sit alongside an elected governor and legislature.
ASM.history: The Samoan islands were settled by Polynesian voyagers thousands of years ago, and the harbor of Pago Pago became a coaling and naval station prized by foreign powers. When the archipelago was divided between Germany and the United States in 1899, the eastern islands became American Samoa under a series of naval governors. The islands remain an unincorporated US territory whose people are US nationals, and its population of under 50,000 has produced a remarkable number of NFL players.
ASM.funFact: American Samoa has sent more players to the NFL per capita than any other place on Earth, producing stars like Troy Polamalu and Junior Seau.

TON.culture: Tonga remains deeply traditional, with a hereditary nobility, Sunday as a strict day of rest and church, and langi-style feasts featuring roast pig and 'ota 'ika raw fish in coconut and lime. Men perform the kailo and women the ma'ulu'ulu seated dance, and tapa bark cloth painted with geometric designs is still made by hand.
TON.history: Polynesians settled Tonga around 3,000 years ago and its rulers built an empire that traded and raided across the South Pacific, with monumental stone trilithons at Ha'amonga built around 1200 AD. Captain Cook named the islands the Friendly Islands in 1773 after a warm welcome, though he may have been walking into a planned feast and ambush. Tonga is the only Pacific nation never formally colonized, uniting under King Taufa'ahau Tupou I in 1845 and keeping its monarchy, which still reigns over the country today.
TON.funFact: Tonga's flag is the only national flag in the world that is just a solid red field with a plain cross in the corner, chosen so no one would ever mistake it for a shipping signal.

famous: World War II wrecks at Guadalcanal
SLB.culture: Solomon Islanders live mostly in small coastal and inland villages, speak over 60 languages and use panpipes, bamboo bands and shell valuables in ceremonies and bride price. Kastom, a blend of ancestral practice and Christianity, governs much of daily life, and rugby league and soccer fill the one stadium in Honiara on weekends.
SLB.history: Austronesian voyagers settled the Solomons thousands of years ago, and early Spanish explorers named the islands after King Solomon's gold, convinced they had found the source of his wealth. British protectorate rule began in 1893, and the islands became a pivot of the Pacific War when US and Japanese forces fought brutally for Guadalcanal between 1942 and 1943, sinking hundreds of ships into what divers now call Iron Bottom Sound. Independence came in 1978, followed by ethnic tensions in the early 2000s that required an Australian-led peacekeeping force before the country returned to stability.
SLB.funFact: Some Solomon Islanders have a gene inherited from Denisovans, an extinct human species, that gives their blonde hair a genetic origin completely different from European blondness.

famous: the world's most accessible live volcano
VUT.culture: Vanuatu's people speak over 100 languages, more per capita than any other country, and share Bislama as a common tongue. Villages practice kastom with grades of pig-tusk-wearing chiefs, kava drinking in nakamal houses, and the spectacular naghol land diving ritual where men leap from towers with vines tied to their ankles.
VUT.history: Austronesian Lapita voyagers reached Vanuatu around 3,000 years ago, and the islands later became a New Hebrides condominium jointly ruled by Britain and France from 1906, a clumsy system with two of everything from police to postage stamps. During World War II up to half a million American troops passed through, and the residents of Tanna even began worshipping an American serviceman named John Frum as a returned god in cargo cults. Vanuatu gained independence in 1980, adopting a name that fused 'vanua' land and 'new', and is now a leader in climate advocacy and in welcoming climate refugees.
VUT.funFact: On Pentecost Island men leap from 30 meter wooden towers with only tree vines tied to their ankles, a harvest ritual that inspired modern bungee jumping.

famous: the first country to see each new day
KIR.culture: I-Kiribati life revolves around the maneaba, a thatched community meeting house where decisions are reached by consensus, and around fishing and coconut palms on atolls barely a meter or two above the sea. Dancing is fierce and precise, with audiences expected to show respect through stillness rather than clapping.
KIR.history: Micronesian and Polynesian voyagers settled the Gilbert and Phoenix islands and Line Islands over centuries, and Britain grouped them as the Gilbert and Ellice Islands protectorate from 1892. The islands saw one of the bloodiest battles of World War II when US Marines stormed Tarawa in 1943, and nuclear tests were carried out at Kiritimati in the 1950s and 1960s. Kiribati became independent in 1979, straightened the country's time zone so it could claim to be the first to greet each new day and millennium, and now faces the existential threat of sea level rise, even purchasing land in Fiji as a possible refuge.
KIR.funFact: Kiribati moved the date line eastward in 1995 so the whole country sits on the same day, making its uninhabited Caroline atoll the first place on Earth to greet the year 2000.

famous: the giant coconut crab and abundant reefs
MHL.culture: Marshallese society is organized around chiefs and clans on tiny atolls, with outrigger canoes, weaving and jajei stick dances. Stick charts made of palm ribs and shells were once used to teach wave patterns for ocean navigation, and a peaceful protest movement against nuclear testing became its own activist tradition.
MHL.history: Micronesian navigators settled the Marshalls thousands of years ago, developing astonishing wayfinding skills using stick charts to read ocean swells. Spain claimed the islands and Germany later ran them as a trading colony, but after World War II the United States used Bikini and Enewetak atolls for 67 nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958, forcibly evacuating islanders and leaving lasting contamination, including the giant Castle Bravo blast of 1954. The Marshalls became independent in free association with the US in 1986 and now speak out globally as a witness to the nuclear age.
MHL.funFact: The two-piece swimsuit is named after Bikini Atoll because its 1946 launch, days before the first nuclear test there, was meant to suggest something explosively exciting.

famous: the ancient ruins of Nan Madol
four island states across a million square miles
FSM.culture: The Federated States of Micronesia spans four states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, each with its own language and traditions. On Yap giant stone discs called rai were quarried on distant islands and serve as traditional currency, while Pohnpei holds sakau kava ceremonies and Chuuk's lagoon is a graveyard of Japanese WWII ships now beloved by divers.
FSM.history: Micronesian voyagers settled these islands over 3,000 years ago, and on Pohnpei they built Nan Madol, a Venice-like city of basalt log islets and canals constructed between roughly 1200 and 1500 AD. Spain, Germany and Japan all claimed the islands in turn, and Japan developed Chuuk into its mightiest naval base in the South Pacific until American aircraft destroyed it in Operation Hailstone in February 1944. After US administration under the UN trust system, the FSM became independent in free association with the United States in 1986, which still provides defense and funding.
FSM.funFact: Nan Madol's basalt columns, some weighing 50 tons, were hauled across water with no modern tools, and locals say the magician Olisihpa and Olosohpa levitated the stones into place.

PLW.culture: Palauan society runs through a ranked system of clans and chiefly councils, with matrilineal lines deciding chiefly titles, and traditional bai meeting houses once painted with story panels. Women hold formal advisory power through their own councils, and a First Traditional Leaders Council still advises the government alongside modern democratic institutions.
PLW.history: Palau's islands were settled by seafarers from Southeast Asia and Indonesia around 3,000 or more years ago, and outsiders found a society of villages linked by ranked clans and famous for its money of carved stone and turtle shell trays. Spain, Germany, Japan and finally the United States all administered the islands in turn, and the waters of Peleliu and Angaur saw fierce WWII fighting in 1944. Palau became independent in free association with the US in 1994 and is now a global leader in ocean conservation, having made its entire exclusive economic zone a marine sanctuary.
PLW.funFact: In Palau's Jellyfish Lake, millions of golden jellyfish have lost their sting over millennia of evolution, so visitors can swim safely among a living mass of them.

NRU.culture: Nauruans love Australian rules football, which is the national sport, and life centers on family networks and church on an island you can drive around in under half an hour. Traditional fishing, swaying palms and songs in Nauruan survive alongside the phosphate economy's complicated legacy.
NRU.history: Micronesian and Polynesian settlers populated Nauru over millennia, and the island stayed isolated until British whalers arrived in the 1830s, followed by devastating colonial conflicts and German rule from 1888. The discovery of rich phosphate from bird droppings made Nauru one of the richest places per capita by the 1970s, run by a trust that included Australia, New Zealand and Britain. Independence came in 1968, but by the 2000s the phosphate was gone, the mined interior was ruined, and the tiny nation struggled with debt and health crises while hosting an Australian offshore processing center.
NRU.funFact: In the 1980s Nauruans were among the fattest and wealthiest people on Earth per capita, and the island even bought a skyscraper in Melbourne nicknamed Nauru House.

TUV.culture: Tuvaluan celebrations center on the fatele, a rhythmic group song with percussion and swaying performed by whole villages at weddings and national days. People live mainly by fishing, growing pulaka root crops in pits, and remittances from relatives working abroad, mostly as sailors.
TUV.history: Polynesian voyagers settled Tuvalu's nine atolls, likely mixing with Micronesian settlers, and the islands became the British Ellice Islands protectorate in 1892, later grouped with the Gilberts. In 1974 the Ellice Islanders voted to separate from the Gilbertese, and Tuvalu became independent in 1978, one of the smallest and most remote countries on Earth. Its highest point is only about four meters above sea level, making Tuvalu a global symbol of climate change vulnerability and a vocal advocate for rising-sea nations.
TUV.funFact: Tuvalu earns a surprising slice of its national income from licensing its .tv internet domain, a windfall that funded everything from electricity to its UN membership.

famous: the tattoo traditions of the Marquesas
PYF.culture: Polynesian life in the islands flows around family, church and the Heiva i Tahiti festival each July, when warriors' drum teams, flower crown parades and outrigger canoe races fill Papeete. Tahitian French fusion food features poisson cru, raw tuna marinated in lime and coconut milk, and the word tattoo itself comes from Tahitian.
PYF.history: Polynesian voyagers settled Tahiti and the surrounding archipelagos over 1,000 years ago, building a sophisticated society of clans, temples called marae and powerful chiefs and priests. British captain Samuel Wallis arrived in 1767, followed by Louis-Antoine de Bougainville who named it Nouvelle Cythere, and missionaries arrived on the Duff in 1797, ending traditional tattooing for a time. France made Tahiti a protectorate in 1842 and later a full colony, and after WWII French Polynesia became an overseas collectivity, though French nuclear testing at Moruroa from 1966 to 1996 left deep resentment.
PYF.funFact: France detonated nearly 200 nuclear devices at Moruroa atoll in French Polynesia between 1966 and 1996, and the tests are still the subject of lawsuits and angry politics today.

NCL.culture: New Caledonia blends Kanak Melanesian custom with French style, so you can watch a coutume ceremony of gifts and speeches in the morning and eat a baguette by the lagoon in the afternoon. Kanak music with wooden percussion and bougna feasts steamed in banana leaves sit alongside boules, wine and bistros in Noumea.
NCL.history: Kanak people settled the main island of Grande Terre around 3,000 years ago, developing complex chiefdoms with war canoes and grand clan houses. France claimed the archipelago in 1853 under Napoleon III and used it as a penal colony for decades, shipping thousands of convicts and political prisoners including Paris Commune rebels. The Kanak independence movement led by Jean-Marie Tjibaou and the FLNKS pushed France to hold three referendums between 2018 and 2021 on independence, which were all narrowly rejected, with a fourth negotiated period under the 1998 Noumea Accord now unfolding.
NCL.funFact: New Caledonia's UNESCO-listed lagoon is so vast, around 24,000 square kilometers, that it can be seen from space, and it shelters dugongs and breeding humpback whales.

famous: the Te Muri coral reefs and black pearls of Manihiki
COK.culture: Cook Islands Maori culture shines through imene tuki singing with deep-throated grunting harmonies, elaborate hip-shaking ura pa'u dance and pareu wrapping. Sunday church services with harmonized hymns, ukuleles and feasting are a highlight of island life.
COK.history: Polynesian voyagers settled the Cooks around 1,500 years ago, and Captain James Cook visited in 1773 and 1777 though he never landed on the main island now bearing his name, which was named by later Russian mapmakers. Missionaries arrived in 1821 and Britain declared a protectorate in 1888, with administration later transferred to New Zealand. The Cook Islands became self-governing in free association with New Zealand in 1965, so Cook Islanders hold New Zealand citizenship and many now live in Auckland, which has a larger Cook Islands population than the islands themselves.
COK.funFact: More Cook Islanders live overseas than at home, with a large community in Auckland, and the islands' population of under 20,000 is smaller than the number of overseas Cook Islanders by far.

famous: the limu reef and chasms like Matapa Chasm
NIU.culture: Niuean village life centers on the church, and the takalo war dance and hifi ulu weaving show a distinct culture from its Tongan and Samoan neighbors. Niuean language and identity are fiercely preserved, and the tiny population of under 2,000 means nearly everyone knows everyone.
NIU.history: Niue was settled by Polynesian voyagers, probably from Tonga and Samoa, around 1,000 years ago and stayed largely isolated, earning the nickname the Rock of Polynesia for its raised coral cliffs. Missionaries arrived in 1846, and in 1900 Niue became a British protectorate, passing to New Zealand administration in 1901. Self-government in free association with New Zealand came in 1974, making it possibly the smallest self-governing state, and Cyclone Heta in 2004 devastated much of the capital Alofi and pushed many Niueans to emigrate.
NIU.funFact: Niue was the first country in the world to offer free wifi nationwide to every citizen, and it plans to someday make its entire exclusive economic zone a marine protected area.

famous: WWII War in the Pacific sites
GUM.culture: Chamorro culture survives in latte stone symbols, fiestas with red rice, kelaguen marinated meat and kadon pika chicken stew, and the respect system of manngge between elders and youth. American military presence and tourism from Japan and Korea mix with Spanish-surnamed Catholic life.
GUM.history: Chamorro seafarers settled Guam around 4,000 years ago and built a society of latte stone houses, proa outrigger canoes and clan lineages. Ferdinand Magellan landed in 1521 and Spain claimed the island in 1565, holding it for centuries until the United States captured it in the Spanish-American War of 1898. Japan seized Guam on the same day as Pearl Harbor in December 1941 and occupied it for over two years, until American forces recaptured it in July 1944 in one of the Pacific War's fiercest campaigns. Guam remains a major US military hub and an unincorporated territory whose people are US citizens but cannot vote for president.
GUM.funFact: The latte stones that appear on Guam's flag and seal are actually the foundation pillars of ancient Chamorro houses, and no one is quite sure how they were moved into place.

famous: the Suicide Cliff and Banzai Cliff WWII sites
MNP.culture: The Northern Marianas blend Chamorro traditions with the distinct culture of Carolinian settlers from the Chuuk area, especially on Saipan where both groups are prominent. Annual fiestas with red rice and kelaguen, Latte Stone symbols and a mixture of American and Asian influences define island life.
MNP.history: Chamorro people settled these islands thousands of years ago, and later waves of Carolinian voyagers from the west added a second Indigenous culture. Spain claimed the islands in the 1600s, Germany bought them after the Spanish-American War and Japan developed them heavily between the world wars, turning Saipan into a major sugar and naval base. The Battle of Saipan in June and July 1944 was one of the Pacific War's bloodiest, with Japanese civilians and soldiers leaping from cliffs rather than surrender. After US administration and UN trusteeship, the islands became a US commonwealth in 1978, and their people are US citizens.
MNP.funFact: The Marianas Trench, the deepest place on Earth at nearly 11 kilometers below sea level, lies just east of these islands and is named after them.

famous: three tiny atolls and one coral lagoon
TKL.culture: Tokelauan life is organized around three villages, one per atoll, with the taupulega council of elders sharing power with a modern government. Fishing, weaving and Sundays in church fill the calendar, and Tokelauan identity is deeply tied to family and land called fanua.
TKL.history: Polynesian voyagers settled Tokelau's atolls of Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo centuries ago, and the islands were once divided among different chiefs and sometimes raided by neighboring groups. British whalers and traders arrived in the 1800s, and Britain declared a protectorate in 1889 before transferring administration to New Zealand in 1925. New Zealand administers Tokelau as a non-self-governing territory, and referendums in 2006 and 2007 narrowly voted against full independence, leaving it as one of the most isolated and smallest communities on Earth with no airport, reachable only by boat from Samoa.
TKL.funFact: Tokelau is the first country or territory to generate almost all its electricity from solar power, switching over in 2012 with a bank of panels that cover a large part of each atoll.

famous: the traditional king and chief system
WLF.culture: Wallis and Futuna keeps an unusual blend of Polynesian custom and French administration, with three traditional kingdoms still holding power alongside the French state. Kava ceremonies, tapa cloth making and Sunday mass are central, and the laka dance and singing are performed with great pride.
WLF.history: Polynesian voyagers settled Wallis around 3,000 years ago, and on Futuna the chiefly tradition of savages and kings developed a distinctive political structure, with the famous Tu'i Tonga connection reflected in local legends. Dutch and French explorers visited in the 1600s and 1700s, and French Marist missionaries arrived in the 1830s, converting the population and signing a protectorate in 1888 with the local kings. Wallis and Futuna became a French overseas territory in 1961 and remains a territory with its own elected assembly and three traditional kings, a truly unusual blend of old and new.
WLF.funFact: Wallis and Futuna has three separate traditional kings who still hold formal power alongside the French state, an arrangement almost nowhere else in the world.

NFK.culture: Norfolk Islanders speak English and Norf'k, a creole descended from the speech of Tahitian women and Bounty mutineers, and hold Thanksgiving and Bounty Day festivals in period costume. Island life moves around fishing, golf, convict-era ruins and the great pines that shade the roads.
NFK.history: Polynesians lived on Norfolk Island around the 1300s and 1400s, then vanished for reasons unknown before Captain James Cook discovered the island in 1774 and reported its fine pines and flax. Britain used it as a fearsome second penal colony from 1825 to 1855, considered the harshest in the Empire, and then in 1856 the whole community of Pitcairn Islanders, descendants of the HMS Bounty mutineers, moved to Norfolk because Pitcairn had grown too small for them. Norfolk Island is now an Australian external territory, though the islanders keep a distinct identity and their own language and flag.
NFK.funFact: In 1856 the entire population of Pitcairn Island, just 194 people descended from Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian wives, packed up and relocated together to Norfolk Island.

famous: world-class diving off the drop zone
one of the world's great seabird islands
CXR.culture: Christmas Island's community is a unique mix of Chinese, Malay, Indian and European backgrounds, so the island celebrates Chinese New Year, Hari Raya, Deepavali and Christmas side by side. Halal food stalls, Buddhist temples and mosques all share a few streets, and the accent is distinctly Australian.
CXR.history: The island was uninhabited when William Dampier charted it in 1688 and Captain William Mynors named it on Christmas Day 1643, and Britain annexed it in 1888 largely for its rich phosphate. Workers came from China, Malaysia and Singapore to mine the phosphate, giving the island its multicultural mix, and Japan occupied the island briefly during WWII. Australia took over administration in 1958 from Singapore, and today the island is famous for its 50 million red crabs that migrate to the sea each wet season, and for the immigration detention center that once made global headlines.
CXR.funFact: Each year tens of millions of red crabs shut down roads on Christmas Island for their breeding migration, and the authorities even close highways and build crab tunnels and bridges for them.

famous: the Cossies family and Clunies-Ross legacy
the world's most remote alfresco territory
CCK.culture: The Cocos community is largely Cocos Malay, descended from workers brought in the 1800s, with a distinct dialect, Islam and a love of badminton and boat life. A small Australian community lives alongside, and the atoll's quiet pace revolves around the tide, the airport and family gatherings.
CCK.history: The uninhabited atoll was charted by Captain William Keeling in 1609 and settled in the 1820s by Alexander Hare and John Clunies-Ross, whose family ruled the islands as a private fiefdom for nearly 150 years, bringing in Malay workers to harvest coconuts. The islands became part of the Straits Settlements under Britain in 1857 and were administered from Singapore, then transferred to Australia in 1955. The Cocos Malays voted in a 1984 referendum for integration with Australia, ending the Clunies-Ross era, and today the islands are an Australian external territory with a small airfield that served as a WWII staging base.
CCK.funFact: The Clunies-Ross family minted their own currency, the Cocos rupee, which could only be spent at the family company store, keeping their workers in effective bondage for generations.

PCN.culture: Pitcairn's few dozen residents, nearly all descended from mutineers and Tahitians, speak a unique creole blending 18th century English and Tahitian. Life revolves around the Seventh-day Adventist church, fishing, growing fruit in fertile volcanic soil and selling carved wood and honey to the rare passing cruise ship.
PCN.history: In 1789 Fletcher Christian led the famous mutiny on HMS Bounty against Captain William Bligh, and after burning the ship the mutineers and their Tahitian companions hid on tiny Pitcairn, which stayed undiscovered until 1808. The community grew from nine mutineers and a group of Tahitian men and women, surviving violence and disease, and in 1838 Britain made Pitcairn a British colony, reportedly the first to give women the vote. Today only around 35 to 50 people live on the island, reachable by a two day boat ride from New Zealand, and it is the least populous territory on Earth.
PCN.funFact: Pitcairn has no airport and no harbor, so visiting ships must anchor offshore while islanders row out in longboats through a gap in the cliffs to trade and load mail.

famous: the Kerguelen Islands, the Desolation Islands
ATF.culture: There is no civilian culture here, only rotating crews of French scientists, technicians and a handful of meteorologists living at Port-aux-Francais on Kerguelen and at Martin-de-Vivies on Amsterdam Island. Life is governed by resupply schedules, expedition routines and shared meals, with the French tricolor flying over islands visited by more penguins than people.
ATF.history: The French Southern and Antarctic Lands are scattered French territories in the subantarctic Indian Ocean, including the Kerguelen Islands found by Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen-Tremarec in 1772, plus Crozet, Amsterdam and Saint Paul islands. Sealers and whalers exploited the islands' wildlife brutally in the 19th century, nearly wiping out fur seals and elephant seals, before France consolidated its claims in the early 20th century. The territory was created as an overseas territory in 1955 and is administered from Reunion by a prefect, hosting French scientific stations that study climate, biology and space tracking.
ATF.funFact: The Kerguelen Islands are so remote, over 3,000 kilometers from the nearest populated land, that early sailors called them the Desolation Islands, and only about 45 to 100 people live there at any time.

famous: king penguin colonies at Salisbury Plain
Ernest Shackleton's epic voyage and grave
SGS.culture: There are no permanent residents, only a small rotating British Government Officer team and museum staff at King Edward Point, plus scientists at Bird Island studying seabirds and seals. The South Georgia Museum in the old whaling station manager's house tells visitors the island's story of whaling, exploration and recovery of wildlife.
SGS.history: Captain James Cook made the first landing in 1775 and claimed the island for Britain, naming it after King George III, and by the early 1900s it became the center of Antarctic whaling, with stations like Grytviken processing thousands of whales. The explorer Ernest Shackleton crossed the island's mountains in 1916 to rescue his crew from Elephant Island, and he is buried at Grytviken, where whalers still visit his grave. Argentina occupied the island briefly in April 1982, and the recapture of South Georgia was the first British victory of the Falklands War. The island is now a British Overseas Territory with no permanent population, famous for wildlife recovery since whaling ended in the 1960s.
SGS.funFact: Rats arrived with whalers and devastated South Georgia's seabirds for two centuries, but a massive baiting campaign completed in 2018 made the island rodent free, allowing pipits and petrels to return.
